conflicts/later-crusades/name: Later crusades to the East: Damietta, Frederick II, Louis IX and the fall of Acre
conflicts/later-crusades/religionRoleNot: These expeditions were preached as penitential wars for the recovery and defence of Jerusalem and the Holy Land, funded by church taxes and rewarded with the plenary indulgence; for leaders such as Louis IX, personal piety was plainly the driving motive. Historians in the ‘pluralist’ school (Riley-Smith, Housley) stress the sincerity of crusading devotion, while others (Tyerman) emphasise how papal finance, dynastic prestige, Italian commerce and the papacy’s parallel crusades against Christian rulers such as Frederick II blurred the ideal. On the Muslim side the Ayyubids and Mamluks also framed the struggle as jihad, especially under Baybars.
conflicts/later-crusades/sides/0/leaders: the Templars, Hospitallers and Teutonic Knights
conflicts/later-crusades/sides/1/name: Ayyubid sultans of Egypt and Syria
conflicts/later-crusades/sides/3/name: Mongol Ilkhanate and Cilician Armenia (intermittent allies of the Franks)
conflicts/later-crusades/sides/3/faith: Mongol shamanism and Buddhism, with Nestorian Christian influence; Armenian Apostolic
conflicts/later-crusades/summary: After the Fourth Crusade the papacy kept launching expeditions to recover Jerusalem. The Fifth Crusade took and lost Damietta in Egypt (1218–1221); Frederick II regained Jerusalem by treaty in 1229 while excommunicate; Louis IX’s great Egyptian crusade ended in his capture in 1250. The rising Mamluk sultanate under Baybars then reduced the crusader states, and the fall of Acre in 1291 ended the Latin presence on the mainland of Syria and Palestine.
conflicts/later-crusades/story:
In 1213 Innocent III issued Quia maior, reorganising crusading so that anyone, even those unfit to fight, could gain an indulgence by contributing money or prayer, and the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 decreed a crusade for 1217 funded by a tax on clerical income. The resulting Fifth Crusade aimed at Egypt, the economic centre of the Ayyubid sultanate. From May 1218 crusaders besieged Damietta in the Nile delta; the city fell in November 1219 after its population had been devastated by famine and disease. Sultan al-Kamil repeatedly offered to return Jerusalem and most of the old kingdom in exchange for Damietta, but the papal legate Pelagius rejected the terms, expecting the arrival of Frederick II. In 1221 the crusaders marched on Cairo, were trapped by the Nile flood near Mansurah and had to surrender Damietta to secure their release.

During the siege, in 1219, Francis of Assisi crossed the lines and preached before al-Kamil, who received him courteously and let him return; the meeting became a lasting symbol of a different Christian approach to Islam. Frederick II, who had taken the cross in 1215, delayed his departure so long that Pope Gregory IX excommunicated him in 1227. Sailing regardless in 1228, he negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa with al-Kamil in February 1229, which returned Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Nazareth to the Christians for ten years while leaving the Temple Mount to Muslims. He crowned himself in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre while the patriarch laid the city under interdict, and papal troops were meanwhile invading his Italian kingdom under the banner of a crusade.

The settlement did not last. In August 1244 Khwarazmian troops allied to the Ayyubid sultan al-Salih Ayyub sacked Jerusalem, killing many Christians, and in October the army of the Latin East was destroyed at La Forbie near Gaza. Louis IX of France took the cross that year. After long preparation, financed largely by church taxes, he sailed from Aigues-Mortes in 1248, wintered in Cyprus and took Damietta in June 1249. At Mansurah in February 1250 his brother Robert of Artois charged recklessly into the town and was killed with many knights; in April the starving, sick army was captured on its retreat, and Louis was ransomed for an enormous sum. A coup in May 1250 killed the sultan Turanshah and brought the Mamluk military slaves to power. Louis stayed in the East until 1254, refortifying the coastal towns.

The Mongols transformed the region: they sacked Baghdad in 1258, killing the caliph, and entered Syria with Armenian and Georgian Christian allies, but in 1260 the Mamluks under Qutuz and Baybars defeated them at Ain Jalut. As sultan (1260–1277) Baybars waged a systematic jihad against the Franks, taking Caesarea and Arsuf in 1265, Safed in 1266, where the Templar garrison was executed after surrendering, and Antioch in 1268, where much of the population was killed or enslaved. Louis IX’s second crusade of 1270 was diverted to Tunis, where he died of disease; the Lord Edward of England’s expedition of 1271–1272 achieved little.

The Second Council of Lyon in 1274 planned a new general crusade and gathered memoranda on why crusading was failing, but Gregory X died in 1276 before it could be launched. The Latin states were divided by the War of St Sabas between Venice and Genoa and by baronial quarrels. Sultan Qalawun took Tripoli in 1289, and when Italian crusaders killed Muslim merchants in Acre in 1290 he prepared a final campaign. His son al-Ashraf Khalil besieged Acre from April 1291; the city fell on 18 May, with many defenders and inhabitants killed or enslaved, and the Templar fortress fell ten days later. Tyre, Sidon, Beirut and the castles of Tortosa and Atlit were abandoned by August.

Crusading did not end in 1291: plans for recovering the Holy Land, the Hospitallers’ conquest of Rhodes, and expeditions such as the capture of Alexandria in 1365 continued for a century. But the loss of Acre ended two centuries of Latin rule on the Syrian mainland, and the military orders were left to justify their existence; the Templars were dissolved in 1312 at the Council of Vienne after their arrest by Philip IV of France.
conflicts/later-crusades/nameOfGod: Crusaders took a vow and wore the cross, receiving the plenary indulgence promised by Quia maior and the Lateran decree Ad liberandam (1215); preaching by Cistercians and then by Franciscan and Dominican friars used model sermons on the cross and the Holy Sepulchre. Louis IX presented his crusades as acts of penance and sought to embody the ideal Christian king. Papal crusades against Frederick II, preached with the same indulgences, showed how the instrument could be turned against Christian rulers. Muslim rulers, especially Baybars, used the language of jihad and recovery of the land of Islam.
conflicts/later-crusades/religiousCauses: The desire to recover Jerusalem, lost in 1187 and briefly regained 1229–1244, as the place of Christ’s passion and the goal of pilgrimage.
Innocent III’s reforms of crusade preaching, indulgences and finance, which made crusading part of ordinary Christian devotion.
The penitential piety of kings such as Louis IX, who saw crusade as service owed to Christ.
On the Muslim side, a renewed ideology of jihad against the Franks and the Mongols, cultivated by the Mamluk sultans.
conflicts/later-crusades/otherCauses/0: Strategic analysis that Egypt was the key to holding Jerusalem, which led crusades to Damietta and Mansurah.
conflicts/later-crusades/otherCauses/1: Dynastic and political ambitions, including Frederick II’s claim to the crown of Jerusalem through his marriage to Isabella II and the conflict between empire and papacy.
conflicts/later-crusades/otherCauses/2: Commercial interests of Venice, Genoa and Pisa in the Levantine ports, and their wars with each other.
conflicts/later-crusades/otherCauses/3: The rise of the Mongols and the Mamluk military state, which changed the balance of power in Syria.
conflicts/later-crusades/triggers/0: Innocent III’s bull Quia maior (1213) and the crusade decree of the Fourth Lateran Council (1215).
conflicts/later-crusades/triggers/1: The Khwarazmian sack of Jerusalem and the disaster at La Forbie in 1244, which led Louis IX to take the cross.
conflicts/later-crusades/triggers/2: Baybars’s conquests of the 1260s and Qalawun’s capture of Tripoli in 1289, culminating in the killing of Muslim merchants at Acre in 1290.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/0/text: Innocent III issues Quia maior calling for a new crusade.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/1/text: The Fourth Lateran Council decrees a crusade and a clerical tax to fund it.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/2/text: Damietta falls to the Fifth Crusade; Francis of Assisi meets Sultan al-Kamil.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/3/text: Trapped by the Nile flood near Mansurah, the Fifth Crusade surrenders Damietta.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/4/text: Excommunicated Frederick II regains Jerusalem by the Treaty of Jaffa with al-Kamil.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/5/text: Khwarazmian troops sack Jerusalem; the Franks are crushed at La Forbie.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/7/text: Defeat at Mansurah; Louis IX is captured and ransomed; the Mamluks seize power in Egypt.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/8/text: The Mamluks defeat the Mongols at Ain Jalut; Baybars becomes sultan.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/9/text: Baybars takes Antioch, killing or enslaving much of its population.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/10/tex: Louis IX dies at Tunis on his second crusade.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/11/tex: The Second Council of Lyon plans a new crusade that never sails.
conflicts/later-crusades/timeline/12/tex: Al-Ashraf Khalil captures Acre on 18 May; the last Frankish mainland towns are abandoned.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/0/foc: Directed the Fifth Crusade after 1219 and rejected al-Kamil’s offer to exchange Jerusalem for Damietta.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/0/out: Widely blamed for the disaster of 1221.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/1/foc: Defended Egypt against the Fifth Crusade, received Francis of Assisi and negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa with Frederick II.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/1/out: Criticised by many Muslims for ceding Jerusalem; died in Damascus in 1238.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/2/foc: Visited the crusader camp at Damietta in 1219 and preached before the sultan.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/2/out: His encounter became a model for peaceful Christian–Muslim engagement; his rule (1221) told friars among Muslims to avoid disputes and live as Christians.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/3/rol: Holy Roman Emperor and king of Jerusalem
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/3/foc: Regained Jerusalem by negotiation in 1229 while excommunicate.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/3/out: Deposed by Innocent IV at the Council of Lyon in 1245; the papacy preached crusades against him and his heirs.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/4/foc: Led the crusade to Egypt (1248–1254) and the crusade to Tunis (1270).
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/4/out: Captured at Mansurah, ransomed, and died at Tunis; canonised in 1297 as the model crusader king.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/5/ori: Kipchak Turk, enslaved and trained as a mamluk
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/5/rol: Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/5/foc: Fought at Mansurah and Ain Jalut and conquered much of the crusader states in the 1260s.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/5/out: Remembered in Arabic tradition as a hero of jihad; died in Damascus in 1277.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/6/foc: Captured Acre in 1291 and completed the expulsion of the Franks from the mainland.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/6/out: Assassinated by his own emirs in 1293.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/7/foc: Excommunicated Frederick II for failing to crusade, and later preached a crusade against him.
conflicts/later-crusades/keyPeople/7/out: Died in 1241 while Frederick’s army threatened Rome.
conflicts/later-crusades/casualties/note: There are no credible overall totals for these campaigns. Chroniclers give large but unreliable numbers for individual disasters, such as the losses at Damietta (where famine and disease reportedly killed most of the besieged city’s population), the destruction of the Frankish army at La Forbie in 1244, the battle of Mansurah and the captivity of 1250, the fall of Antioch in 1268 and the fall of Acre in 1291. Modern historians treat these figures as indications of scale rather than counts.
conflicts/later-crusades/effects/0: The crusader states on the Syrian and Palestinian mainland were extinguished by 1291, leaving Cyprus and, later, Rhodes as Latin outposts.
conflicts/later-crusades/effects/1: The Mamluk sultanate emerged as the dominant power in Egypt and Syria for more than two centuries, partly legitimised by its wars against Franks and Mongols.
conflicts/later-crusades/effects/2: Eastern Christian communities in the Levant suffered reprisals and pressure as suspected allies of the Franks and Mongols.
conflicts/later-crusades/effects/3: Crusading finance accelerated papal and royal taxation systems in the West.
conflicts/later-crusades/effectsOnChurch: Crusade preaching and the indulgence became part of everyday Western devotion through the friars’ sermons and the commutation of vows for money, which drew growing criticism.
The papacy’s crusades against Frederick II and the Hohenstaufen damaged the moral authority of crusading and of the popes themselves.
Franciscan and Dominican missions to Muslims and Mongols developed alongside crusade, with Francis’s visit to al-Kamil as their emblem.
The loss of the Holy Land contributed to the trial and suppression of the Knights Templar (1307–1312).
conflicts/later-crusades/legacy: The thirteenth-century crusades show both the deepest crusading piety, in Louis IX, and its contradictions: a Holy City regained by an excommunicated emperor through diplomacy, crusades preached against Christian rulers, and repeated failure that critics read as divine judgement on the crusaders’ sins. The fall of Acre in 1291 became a fixed point in Muslim and Christian memory.
conflicts/later-crusades/dissenters/0/te: Went unarmed to Sultan al-Kamil in 1219; early sources say he warned the crusaders before a disastrous attack that it would fail, and his rule urged friars among ‘Saracens’ to live peaceably and confess their faith without quarrels.
conflicts/later-crusades/dissenters/1/te: The St Albans chronicler condemned the papacy’s crusades against Frederick II and the selling of crusade vows, reporting that many believed the defeats in the East were caused by such abuses.
conflicts/later-crusades/dissenters/2/te: The former Dominican master general, in his memorandum for the Council of Lyon (1274), recorded contemporary objections that crusading was contrary to the gospel, that it killed rather than converted, and that God showed displeasure through defeats, even though he himself defended crusading.
conflicts/later-crusades/dissenters/3/te: The Franciscan scholar argued in his Opus maius (1267) that war rarely converts unbelievers and that preaching and learning their languages would do more good.
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/0/tit: The Fifth Crusade in the Nile delta
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/0/peo: Crusaders under John of Brienne and the legate Pelagius
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/0/tex: Sailing from Acre in 1218, the crusaders besieged and took Damietta, then in July 1221 marched south toward Cairo and were cut off by the rising Nile and Ayyubid forces near Mansurah.
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/1/peo: Emperor Frederick II and his army
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/1/tex: Excommunicated, Frederick sailed from Brindisi via Cyprus to Acre, negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa and entered Jerusalem in March 1229 without a battle.
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/2/peo: Louis IX and the French crusade army
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/2/tex: Louis sailed from his new port of Aigues-Mortes, wintered in Cyprus, captured Damietta, was defeated at Mansurah and captured on the retreat, and after his ransom spent four years strengthening the Frankish coast from Acre.
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/3/tit: Louis IX’s last crusade to Tunis
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/3/peo: Louis IX, his sons and the French army
conflicts/later-crusades/campaigns/3/tex: Diverted to Tunis, perhaps in hope of converting its emir or securing a base, the army camped at Carthage, where dysentery killed Louis on 25 August 1270.
